Padon
PAY-don
n. (proper name; head of a family of Nethinim who returned from Babylon)
Hebrew Padon, probably from padah, to ransom or redeem — the verb used of the redemption of the firstborn.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · In the Text · Related

Biblical Definition

Padon appears twice, in the two copies of one register: “The children of Keros, the children of Siaha, the children of Padon” (Ezra 2:44), with Nehemiah 7:47. His family belonged to the Nethinim — the given ones, the temple servants whose descent Joshua traced to the Gibeonites made hewers of wood and drawers of water for the house of God. The Authorized Version uses the name twice and says nothing else. The dictionary notes the name's root, which is padah, to redeem by paying a price: the verb of Exodus 13:13, every firstborn of man among thy children shalt thou redeem, and of Psalm 130:8, he shall redeem Israel from all his iniquities. A family of temple servants, descended from a people spared by a treaty, bearing a name built on the word for ransom, went up out of Babylon to serve in the house of God. Scripture lists them with the priests and the Levites and the singers and the porters, by name and by household, which is the point: the lowest order of temple service was registered as carefully as the highest.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) gives no entry for Padon; the name heads a family of Nethinim, the temple servants, in the register of the return.

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.

expand to see more

The Nethinim are sometimes presented as a servile caste, evidence of a stratified and oppressive temple system. Scripture registers them by household among the returning people, assigns them dwellings in Ophel, and exempts them from tribute by the decree of Artaxerxes. They are servants of the house of God, and the register treats them as part of the nation.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is in the root of the name. Padah is to redeem by price, and Psalm 130:8 says He shall redeem Israel from all his iniquities. A people descended from spared Gibeonites, serving in the temple, bearing redemption in their family name, is the gospel in a register.

Hebrew padah, to ransom or redeem by paying a price.

The same verb is used of redeeming the firstborn in Exodus 13:13.

Ezra 2:44 and Nehemiah 7:47 are the only occurrences of Padon.

The Nethinim are the given ones, servants of the temple.

Psalm 130:8 uses the root of the LORD redeeming Israel from all iniquities.
